25-735.question: Whether the Veterans' Judicial Review Act (VJRA) stripped district courts of jurisdiction, recognized in *Johnson v. Robison* (1974), to hear challenges to the constitutionality of acts of Congress affecting veterans' benefits.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Veterans can't bring constitutional challenges to laws affecting veterans' benefits in district court and must go through the veterans' benefits review system.

options.label: No
options.meaning: District courts can still hear constitutional challenges to laws affecting veterans' benefits.

25-735.background:
Federal district courts have "original jurisdiction of all civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States." [28 U.S.C. § 1331](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/1331). Therefore, by default, they can review constitutional challenges to statutes unless some other statute withdraws that jurisdiction expressly or by implication.

Veterans with service-connected disabilities can apply for monthly benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Since the 1930s, federal law—in a section known as the "no-review clause"—has barred federal courts from reviewing the VA's benefits decisions. The version in effect in 1974 provided that:

> "[T]he decisions of the Administrator on any question of law or fact under any law administered by the Veterans' Administration providing benefits for veterans . . . shall be final and conclusive and no other official or any court of the United States shall have power or jurisdiction to review any such decision[.]"

In [*Johnson v. Robison*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/415/361/) (1974), the Supreme Court held this earlier version of that clause did not stop federal courts from reviewing the constitutionality of veterans' benefits legislation, but instead only restricted judicial review of individual administrative decisions made by the VA. The Court reasoned that the clause covered decisions made "under" a law the VA administered, and a challenge to the law's constitutionality arises under the Constitution instead.

In 1988, Congress passed the [VJRA](https://www.congress.gov/100/statute/STATUTE-102/STATUTE-102-Pg4105.pdf), which—among other things—created a new path for appealing benefits decisions: from the Board of Veterans' Appeals (BVA) to a new Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC), and then to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which it gave exclusive authority over challenges to the validity of veterans' benefits statutes in appeals from the CAVC. It also rewrote the language of the "no-review clause," now at [38 U.S.C. § 511(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/511), to read as follows:

> "The Secretary shall decide all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the Secretary under a law that affects the provision of benefits by the Secretary to veterans . . . . Subject to [certain exceptions, including review through the VJRA's appeals scheme], the decision of the Secretary as to any such question shall be final and conclusive and may not be reviewed by any other official or by any court[.]"
25-735.facts:
Floyd Johnson, a U.S. Army veteran, began receiving disability benefits for service-related post-traumatic stress disorder while serving a 40-year prison sentence in Florida. While the VA approved an 80 percent disability rating and associated benefits, it later reduced his benefits to the level of a 10 percent disability rating. It cited a benefits cap at [38 U.S.C. § 5313](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/5313), which limits disability compensation for veterans incarcerated for more than 60 days following a felony conviction.

Johnson sued Congress, arguing that the law violates the Constitution's [bill of attainder clause](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S9-C3-2/ALDE_00013187/) (which prohibits laws that punish a specific group without a trial), as well as the [Fifth Amendment](https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-5/)'s guarantee of equal protection. He did not challenge how the VA handled his own claim. The district court assumed it had jurisdiction to hear the case but dismissed it on the merits. On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit held that Congress couldn't be sued due to sovereign immunity, but it did not grant Johnson's request to substitute the VA as a defendant. Instead, it vacated the judgment and ordered the case dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, ruling that the VJRA strips district courts of jurisdiction to hear constitutional challenges to veterans' benefits legislation.
25-735.petitioner:
District courts can still hear constitutional challenges to laws affecting veterans' benefits.

- **The plain text of the "no-review clause" doesn't bar these challenges.** The clause only bars review of questions necessary to a decision "under a law." Deciding a benefits claim under a law means assuming its validity and applying it; asking whether the law is constitutional is a question under the Constitution. Congress kept the key words *Robison* interpreted, and when Congress reenacts interpreted language, it is presumed to adopt that interpretation. The VJRA did rewrite other parts of the clause, but the key changes responded to *Traynor v. Turnage* (1988), in which the Supreme Court held that the clause didn't bar a suit alleging that a VA regulation violated the Rehabilitation Act, a law that applies to all federal agencies. Committee reports suggesting otherwise can't override the text.
- **Context and structure support this reading.** If the clause covered constitutional challenges, the BVA would have to decide them, but it was well established when the VJRA was written that the BVA could not. The BVA, which issues the Secretary's final decisions, has long said it lacks that authority, and VA regulations bind the BVA to applicable statutes. The VJRA expressly gave the CAVC and the Federal Circuit power over constitutional questions but gave the BVA none, consistent with the Supreme Court's repeated statements that agencies are poorly suited to judge the constitutionality of their own statutes.
- **The VJRA doesn't create an implied bar either.** Courts evaluate whether a law implicitly strips jurisdiction from district courts and routes claims to a specialized system using the three factors laid out in [*Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/510/200/) (1994). If that test applies, every factor favors district courts: (1) the VA system offers no meaningful review of these challenges, which would sit for years before a BVA that cannot grant relief; (2) constitutional challenges are separate from individual benefits decisions; and (3) the VA has no expertise in constitutional law.
- **Any doubt should be resolved in veterans' favor,** under the pro-veteran canon that ambiguous veterans' benefits laws are read for the veteran. Johnson's reading is the pro-veteran one: sending constitutional challenges to the BVA would leave veterans waiting years, often only for the BVA to decline to decide the question.
25-735.respondent:
Congress frequently replaces district-court jurisdiction with specialized forums, either explicitly or implicitly. The VJRA did so here.

- **The "no-review clause" specifically covers constitutional claims.** A "decision by the Secretary" means the ultimate determination in a matter, such as the amount of benefits a veteran receives. Whether the statute guiding that determination is constitutional is a necessary underlying question of law; a contrary reading would imply that the VA must apply even blatantly unconstitutional statutes.
- **The VJRA's appeals scheme covers constitutional claims, making *Robison* obsolete.** While the BVA has sometimes disavowed authority to decide constitutional challenges, it has also resolved constitutional challenges on several occasions (including past challenges to Section 5313). The statute explicitly authorizes the CAVC to set aside decisions found to be contrary to constitutional right, and it gives the Federal Circuit exclusive jurisdiction to review challenges to the validity of any statute on appeal from the CAVC. This pathway to judicial review resolves the gap that concerned the *Robison* Court, which was that there was no statutory provision at the time authorizing judicial review of the VA's benefits decisions.
- **The VJRA's legislative history shows clear intent to strip district courts of jurisdiction.** The House committee report explained that, under the VJRA, "district courts would no longer have jurisdiction to entertain challenges to the constitutionality of any matter affecting veterans benefits," and stated that "all questions involving benefits laws administered by the VA . . . would include . . . constitutional questions."
- **At minimum, the VJRA implicitly routes constitutional claims to a specialized system.** Courts evaluate whether a law implicitly strips jurisdiction from district courts and routes claims to a specialized system using the three factors laid out in [*Thunder Basin Coal Co. v. Reich*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/510/200/) (1994). If that test applies, every factor favors the VA system: (1) the system provides meaningful judicial review through the CAVC and Federal Circuit; (2) Johnson's challenge is not an independent constitutional issue but is fundamentally tied to a benefits decision that was clearly routed to the VJRA's appeals scheme; and (3) the VA has the expertise from applying this law to consider constitutional challenges.
- **The pro-veteran canon does not apply.** The canon only applies when there are competing and equally plausible interpretations of the statutory text, which is not the case here. Additionally, Johnson's argument is not necessarily pro-veteran, since his argument implies that the VA lacks authority to consider constitutional challenges to federal statutes.

25-170.question:
(1) Whether the Supreme Court has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear this case.
(2) Whether federal law precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate.

options.label: No jurisdiction
options.meaning: The Supreme Court can't decide the case, so the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling letting the suit go forward stands.

options.label: Jurisdiction; claims precluded
options.meaning: Federal law bars Boulder's state-law climate claims, ending the suit.

options.label: Jurisdiction; claims may proceed
options.meaning: Boulder's state-law climate claims can go forward in Colorado court.

25-498.question: Whether, for claims predicated on fund underperformance, pleading that a fiduciary under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) failed to use the requisite "care, skill, prudence, or diligence" under the circumstances and thus breached ERISA's duty of prudence when investing plan assets requires alleging a "meaningful benchmark."

options.label: Yes, a benchmark is required
options.meaning: Plaintiffs claiming imprudent investing based on poor returns must point to a comparable investment that did better.

options.label: No benchmark required
options.meaning: Plaintiffs can state a claim without a specific comparison, based on the circumstances as a whole.

25-579.question:
(1) Whether the federal government's submission to a state or territorial regulator of an application to renew a permit under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) is "final agency action" that is immediately reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
(2) Whether the federal government must comply with the general environmental-review procedures of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) before submitting a permit-renewal application under RCRA, which sets forth its own specific procedures to review environmental impacts in the context of hazardous-waste treatment.

options.label: Not reviewable yet
options.meaning: The Air Force's submission of its permit-renewal application isn't final agency action, so it can't be challenged now.

options.label: Reviewable; NEPA not required
options.meaning: The Air Force's permit-renewal application can be challenged now, but it doesn't need NEPA review because RCRA has its own procedures.

options.label: Reviewable; NEPA required
options.meaning: The Air Force's permit-renewal application can be challenged now, and the Air Force must complete NEPA review before applying.

25-5343.question: Whether *Stinson v. United States* still correctly states the rule for the deference that courts must give the commentary to the Sentencing Guidelines.

options.label: Stinson stands
options.meaning: Courts keep following the commentary unless it is inconsistent with the Guideline it interprets or plainly wrong.

options.label: Kisor's limits apply
options.meaning: Courts follow the commentary only when a Guideline is genuinely ambiguous and the commentary's reading is reasonable.

options.label: No deference
options.meaning: Courts decide what the Guidelines mean themselves, treating the commentary as persuasive at most.

25-5343.facts:
Kendrick Beaird pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a convicted felon. The district court applied a sentencing enhancement because Beaird's gun could accept a "large capacity magazine." The Guidelines do not define that term, but the commentary says it covers any magazine holding more than 15 rounds, and Beaird's held 17. Beaird objected to the court's reliance on the commentary's definition. The district court sentenced him to 72 months in prison, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that *Stinson* was unaffected by *Kisor*.

At the Supreme Court, Beaird argues that the commentary deserves no deference. The government argues that, after *Kisor*, courts should defer only after finding genuine ambiguity in the Guidelines. The Supreme Court appointed an outside lawyer to defend the Fifth Circuit's view that the commentary controls unless it is inconsistent with the Guidelines or plainly wrong.
25-5343.background:
In 1984, Congress created the U.S. Sentencing Commission—an independent agency in the judicial branch—to write rules making federal sentences more uniform. Since 1987, the Commission has published the Federal Sentencing Guidelines, along with official commentary that explains and interprets them. Judges must begin every federal sentencing by correctly calculating the range the Guidelines recommend. In [*Stinson v. United States*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/508/36/) (1993), the Supreme Court held that the commentary is a mandatory part of that calculation unless it violates the Constitution or a federal law or is plainly wrong or inconsistent with the Guideline it interprets. In 2005, the Supreme Court made the Guidelines advisory, so while judges must still begin sentencing by calculating the recommended range, they may choose sentences outside that range.

In [*Kisor v. Wilkie*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/588/18-15/) (2019), the Supreme Court narrowed a similar rule for federal agencies' readings of their own regulations, allowing deference to an agency's interpretation only when a regulation is genuinely ambiguous. Federal appeals courts have disagreed about whether those limits also apply to the commentary.

25-459.question: Whether the phrase "goods or services from a video tape service provider," as used in the Video Privacy Protection Act's (VPPA) definition of "consumer," refers to all of a video tape service provider's goods or services or only to its audiovisual goods or services.

options.label: All goods and services
options.meaning: A newsletter subscriber can be a protected "consumer," so sharing his video-viewing history can create liability under the VPPA.

options.label: Only audiovisual goods and services
options.meaning: Only subscribers to video goods or services count, so a newsletter subscriber isn't protected under the VPPA.

25-5930.question: Whether a claim regarding application of time credits under the First Step Act (FSA), seeking accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement, can be brought in a habeas petition under the federal habeas corpus statute.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Prisoners can use habeas to challenge how First Step Act time credits affect their transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Prisoners must bring challenges to First Step Act time credits another way, such as a civil-rights suit.

25-352.question: Whether a defendant who has filed an answer without pleading an affirmative defense may nonetheless assert that affirmative defense as the basis for a summary judgment motion without amending or seeking to amend its answer to plead that affirmative defense, and whether they may do so even if an amendment adding that affirmative defense would be barred by the court's scheduling order deadline under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(4).

options.label: Yes, even after the amendment deadline
options.meaning: A defendant can raise an unpleaded defense at summary judgment without amending, even when the deadline to amend has passed.

options.label: Yes, but only before the amendment deadline
options.meaning: A defendant can raise an unpleaded defense at summary judgment without amending, but only before the deadline to amend has passed.

options.label: No
options.meaning: A defendant must amend its answer to include the defense before relying on it.

25-1003.question: Whether, under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA), a claim relies on "a new rule of constitutional law . . . that was previously unavailable" when the habeas petitioner could have asserted a claim based on the rule in a prior federal habeas petition.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: A prisoner can bring a second habeas petition based on a new rule even if a claim based on it could have been raised earlier.

options.label: No
options.meaning: If a claim based on the new rule could have been raised in an earlier petition, the rule wasn't "previously unavailable," and the second petition is barred.

25-159.question: Whether "just compensation" should be determined by reference to state law when a private company uses the Natural Gas Act (NGA) to seize someone's land for natural gas infrastructure.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Landowners get compensation measured by state law, which is often more generous.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Landowners get only the minimum compensation the Fifth Amendment requires.

25-417.question: Whether a federal prisoner can sue prison officials for money damages under the Bivens doctrine for deliberate indifference to a non-life-threatening injury.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The prisoner's damages suit can go forward under Bivens.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Bivens doesn't extend to the prisoner's claim, so the damages suit is dismissed.

25-581.question:
(1) Whether a law lacks general applicability under the Free Exercise Clause only if it permits unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for comparable secular conduct.
(2) Whether the rule against excluding religious institutions from public benefits applies only to explicit government bans on participation by religious people and institutions.

options.label: St. Mary wins both
options.meaning: Colorado's rule fails both tests, so excluding the Catholic preschools faces strict scrutiny.

options.label: St. Mary wins on general applicability only
options.meaning: Colorado's exemptions make its preschool rule not generally applicable, but the rule against excluding religious institutions from public benefits doesn't apply.

options.label: St. Mary wins on public benefits only
options.meaning: The rule against excluding religious institutions from public benefits applies, but Colorado's preschool rule still counts as generally applicable.

options.label: Colorado wins both
options.meaning: Colorado can exclude the Catholic preschools.

25-966.question:
(1) Whether Article III of the Constitution precludes the Department of Labor from adjudicating proceedings to collect monetary remedies from employers who have allegedly violated the terms and conditions of employment of H-2A workers and domestic workers in corresponding employment and instead requires them to be decided by a federal court.
(2) Whether the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorizes the Department of Labor to adjudicate such proceedings.

options.label: Labor Department wins both
options.meaning: The Department can keep deciding these H-2A penalty cases itself.

options.label: The INA doesn't authorize it
options.meaning: The INA doesn't give the Labor Department power to decide these H-2A penalty cases, so they must go to court.

options.label: Article III bars it
options.meaning: Even if the INA authorizes the Labor Department to decide these H-2A penalty cases, the Constitution requires a federal court to decide them.

25-842.question: Whether noncitizens who were "granted asylum," but whose asylum was later terminated, are eligible for adjustment to lawful permanent resident status under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), or are categorically ineligible.

options.label: Eligible
options.meaning: People whose asylum was terminated can still seek permanent residence if they meet the other requirements.

options.label: Categorically ineligible
options.meaning: Termination of asylum ends the path to permanent residence through asylum.

25-1017.question:
(1) Whether the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) or a federal consent decree prohibits Arizona from requiring voter-registration applicants to produce "satisfactory evidence" of U.S. citizenship when registering with a state registration form.
(2) Whether the NVRA prohibits Arizona from implementing a program within 90 days of a federal election to cancel the registrations of voters who are not U.S. citizens.

options.label: Arizona wins both
options.meaning: Arizona can require proof of citizenship on its state registration form and can run its citizenship-based removal program close to a federal election.

options.label: Arizona wins proof of citizenship only
options.meaning: Arizona can require proof of citizenship on its state registration form, but can't run its citizenship-based removal program within 90 days of a federal election.

options.label: Arizona wins voter rolls only
options.meaning: Arizona can run its citizenship-based removal program within 90 days of a federal election, but can't require proof of citizenship on its state registration form.

options.label: Arizona loses both
options.meaning: The NVRA or the consent decree blocks both Arizona's proof-of-citizenship requirement and its removal program.

25-965.question: Whether the First Amendment's established chilling-effect doctrine—under which a credible government threat that deters the exercise of fundamental rights constitutes a complete and independently actionable constitutional injury—allows a plaintiff to bring a lawsuit based on government threats both before and after a Planning Commission meeting that chilled religious exercise, worship, and assembly, even when the city had not completed a final land-use decision.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The plaintiff can sue over chilling threats from a city government even without waiting for a final land-use decision.

options.label: No
options.meaning: The plaintiff cannot sue over chilling threats from a city government until the city completes a final land-use decision.

25-1311.question: Whether a court may hold a party in civil contempt based on a violation of an injunction's "spirit" where the injunction is silent as to the conduct upon which contempt is based; or, instead, whether a court must ground a finding of civil contempt on the violation of an order that clearly and unambiguously proscribes the precise conduct at issue.

options.label: Spirit is enough
options.meaning: A court can hold a party in contempt for conduct that undermines an injunction's purpose, even if the injunction doesn't expressly forbid it.

options.label: Clear terms are required
options.meaning: Contempt requires violating an order that clearly and specifically prohibits the conduct.

25-1311.facts:
Apple's App Store is the only way to download apps onto iPhones in the United States. Apple takes a 15-30% commission on digital goods purchased through the App Store, and its anti-steering provisions blocked developers from directing users to cheaper purchasing options outside the App Store.

In 2020, Epic Games, one of the largest mobile game developers and distributor of its own competing app marketplace, sued Apple under federal antitrust law and California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL). The district court rejected the federal claims but agreed that the anti-steering rules violated the UCL by preventing consumers from learning about lower-priced alternatives. It issued a 75-word [permanent injunction](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.364265/gov.uscourts.cand.364265.813.0_3.pdf) barring Apple from prohibiting developers from including buttons, external links, or other calls to action directing users to alternative purchasing mechanisms. The injunction said nothing about commissions. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court declined review in January 2024.

That same day, Apple announced that it would comply by allowing developers to add links. However, Apple would charge up to a 27% commission on purchases made through external links, and it limited how the links looked and where they appeared.

Epic asked the district court to hold Apple in civil contempt, arguing that the commission and restrictions defeated the injunction's purpose even though the text never addressed commissions. In April 2025, the court agreed, finding that Apple had picked the most anticompetitive option it considered and had willfully violated the injunction. The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding, reasoning that a party can be held in contempt for violating an injunction's spirit, not only its words.

24-1016.question: Whether trademark strength is a question of fact or law in a trademark infringement likelihood-of-confusion analysis under the Lanham Act.

options.label: Question of fact
options.meaning: Trademark strength is decided like other facts (including mixed questions that are mainly factual), and appeals courts review it deferentially.

options.label: Question of law
options.meaning: Trademark strength is a legal question that appeals courts decide for themselves.

25-6623.question: Whether the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee a defendant charged with a serious felony the right to a trial by a 12-person jury.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Defendants charged with serious felonies are entitled to 12-person juries, so Florida's six-person felony juries are unconstitutional.

options.label: No
options.meaning: States may keep using smaller juries in felony trials.

25-183.question: Whether Title IX provides employees of federally funded educational institutions a private right of action to sue for sex discrimination in employment.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Employees of federally funded schools and universities can sue for sex discrimination under Title IX.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Employees of federally funded schools and universities can't sue for sex discrimination under Title IX and must rely on other laws, such as Title VII.

25-246.question: Whether, in determining whether a fine contravenes the Excessive Fines Clause, courts may consider the gravity of the underlying offense purely in the abstract or should consider the gravity of the specific defendant's wrongdoing.

options.label: In the abstract
options.meaning: Courts may judge how serious the offense is in general terms when deciding whether a forfeiture is excessive.

options.label: The owner's specific conduct
options.meaning: Courts must look at what the particular owner actually did when deciding whether a forfeiture is excessive.

25-238.question: Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The Second Amendment protects possessing AR-15-style rifles, putting bans like Cook County's in doubt.

options.label: No
options.meaning: The Second Amendment doesn't protect possessing AR-15-style rifles, so bans like Cook County's can stand.

25-566.question: Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The Second Amendment protects possessing AR-15-style rifles, putting bans like Connecticut's in doubt.

options.label: No
options.meaning: The Second Amendment doesn't protect possessing AR-15-style rifles, so bans like Connecticut's can stand.

25-1349.question: Whether the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act (USFSPA) requires state courts to refuse enforcement of indemnification provisions in divorce settlement agreements.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: State courts can't enforce a divorce agreement's promise to make up the ex-spouse's lost share when retirement pay is replaced by disability pay.

options.label: No
options.meaning: State courts can enforce indemnification promises that the veteran agreed to in a divorce settlement.

25-1131.question: Whether a land-use regulation that prohibits a religious institution from building a religious structure on its own property constitutes a "substantial burden" on religious exercise under the Substantial Burden Provision of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA).

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Barring a religious institution from building a religious structure on its own land substantially burdens religious exercise, so the rule must meet RLUIPA's strict test.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Barring a religious institution from building a religious structure on its own land isn't automatically a substantial burden; the institution has to show more.

25-840.question: Whether parents have standing to challenge a state law that requires youth shelters to notify a state child-welfare agency, rather than the parents directly, when a runaway minor seeks gender-affirming care.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The parents can challenge Washington's law in federal court.

options.label: No
options.meaning: The parents lack standing to challenge Washington's law, so the suit is dismissed without a ruling on the law itself.

25-7026.question: Whether an appeals court must grant a petitioner permission to appeal under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) where the petitioner's argument has been foreclosed by binding circuit precedent but has been resolved in the petitioner's favor by another circuit.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: When circuits disagree, a prisoner gets permission to appeal even if their own circuit's precedent is against them.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Binding circuit precedent against the prisoner is enough to deny permission to appeal.

25-1343.question: Whether material support to a terrorist organization, which makes an alien removable and ineligible for various immigration benefits—including asylum—under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), must advance the organization's actual commission of terrorism to qualify for that bar.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The material-support bar applies only if the support helped the organization carry out terrorism.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Any material support to a terrorist organization—such as cooking meals for the organization's leaders—triggers the bar, even if it didn't advance a terrorist act.

25-1103.question: Whether a court may order broad discovery against an Executive Office advisory body—potentially providing much information sought on the merits of a plaintiff's Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) claims—to determine whether FOIA's disclosure requirements apply in the first place.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The court can order broad discovery against DOGE to decide whether FOIA applies to it.

options.label: No
options.meaning: The court can't order broad discovery against DOGE just to decide whether FOIA applies to it.

26-12.question: Whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: A challenge fails unless the targeted group, overall, fared worse relative to its share of applicants.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Evidence of discriminatory intent can support a challenge even without that overall statistical showing.

26-104.question: Whether the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) mandates the detention pending removal proceedings of aliens who, like the respondent, are present in the United States without having been admitted.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: People who entered without being admitted must be detained while their removal cases proceed, without bond hearings.

options.label: No
options.meaning: People who entered without being admitted aren't subject to mandatory detention and may seek release on bond.

26-204.question: Whether the federal ban on distilling spirits in a home, or in a shed or yard connected to a home, is a valid use of Congress's taxing power and the Necessary and Proper Clause.

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: The ban on home distilling is a valid exercise of Congress's taxing power.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Congress lacks the power to ban home distilling this way.

26-426.question:
(1) Whether the district court had jurisdiction to hear the challenge.
(2) Whether the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) allowed the district court to enter classwide declaratory relief and set aside the government's guidance on removing noncitizens to countries not named in their removal orders.
(3) Whether that guidance, including its procedures for notice and for raising a fear of persecution or torture, is lawful under the INA, the Due Process Clause, or the Convention Against Torture (CAT) as implemented by the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act (FARRA) and its regulations.

options.label: No jurisdiction
options.meaning: The district court couldn't hear the challenge, so its judgment is undone.

options.label: Jurisdiction; no classwide relief
options.meaning: The district court could hear the challenge but couldn't grant classwide relief or set aside the guidance.

options.label: Classwide relief allowed; guidance lawful
options.meaning: The district court could grant classwide relief, but the government's third-country removal guidance is lawful.

options.label: Classwide relief allowed; guidance unlawful
options.meaning: The district court's judgment setting aside the government's third-country removal guidance stands.

25-1223.question: Whether a noncitizen who wins a habeas case challenging civil immigration detention can recover attorney's fees from the government under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA).

options.label: Yes
options.meaning: Noncitizens who win habeas challenges to their immigration detention can recover attorney's fees under EAJA.

options.label: No
options.meaning: Noncitizens who win habeas challenges to their immigration detention can't recover attorney's fees under EAJA.

options.label: Enforce arbitration
options.meaning: The consumers' automatic-stay claims go to arbitration under their card agreements.

options.label: Bankruptcy court may keep the claims
options.meaning: The bankruptcy court can refuse to send the consumers' automatic-stay claims to arbitration.

25-1408.question: Whether, and under what circumstances, a bankruptcy court may refuse to enforce a valid arbitration agreement under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) for claims seeking damages for violations of the Bankruptcy Code's automatic stay.
